answer: In the Quran 5:21 Moses tells his people to enter the holy land God assigned them; in 5:24-26 they refuse and it is forbidden to them for forty years. 7:137 and 10:93 say God made the oppressed people heirs of blessed lands and settled them in one; 17:104 says to dwell in the land and that He will bring them together at the Hereafter's promise, read by al-Jalalayn as the Hour. None names the land; commentators say Syria, Palestine or Jerusalem. Muslim scholars differ: Atiyyah Saqr of Al-Azhar and Sheikh Ahmad Saad held the promise lapsed with disobedience (Saqr's fatwa also predicts the Jews will not remain); al-Hussaini holds it unbroken. Genesis 17:8 gives Canaan to Abraham's descendants 'for an everlasting possession' (17:21 places the covenant with Isaac). Jerusalem and al-Aqsa are sacred in Islam: the Night Journey, the first direction of prayer.

facts.text: Three Muslim voices hold that the Israelites' claim was conditional on obedience or has passed away. Atiyyah Saqr (former head of the Al-Azhar fatwa committee) writes that it stands only while the people obey God; the same fatwa also says that the Jews 'have occupied Palestine, they will never remain there forever' and hopes for 'another defeat and severe blow' at Muslim hands, citing Quran 7:167. An article by Noah Ali Salman on the Jordanian General Iftaa' Department site says the Children of Israel were stripped of 'the honor of the trust' because of their sins and that the earth's 'final outcome belongs to the righteous'; it is framed as seeking clarity on 'the end of the battle between us and the Jews'. Sheikh Ahmad Saad, answering a reader on About Islam, says that 'as soon as they deviated, the holy land was not theirs anymore because they are no longer fulfilling Allah's law'. A survey by Ersin Çelik finds some contemporary commentators call the land a temporary dwelling during the exodus, not an eternal homeland.

facts.text: Three Muslim voices are reported to read the Quran as granting the land to the Jews lastingly, but only the first is read in his own words. Muhammad al-Hussaini, in his own Middle East Quarterly essay, says 'there are no grounds in religious law to entertain the conceit that God's promise to the Children of Israel has been broken'. The Jordanian Sheikh Ahmad al-Adwan, in an interview with Mida magazine as relayed by The Algemeiner (we read the relay, not the interview), says 'I recognize their sovereignty over their land' and cites Quran 5:21. The Italian imam Abdul Hadi Palazzi argues in an essay in Tablet that the Quran supports the biblical claim; we read only First Things' summary of it, not the essay.

contested.text: How the verses are read is a dispute inside Islam, not between Islam and outsiders. Atiyyah Saqr holds that the promise lasted only while the people obeyed God and no longer exists; Çelik's survey finds that most classical commentators take the holy land to mean Jerusalem and that some contemporary ones call it a temporary dwelling; al-Hussaini reads the Quran as awarding the land to the Jews for all time.

Spencer says the majority of Muslims cite other verses and hadith against a Jewish claim, and that the Hamas charter, which calls Palestine an Islamic waqf (religious endowment) consecrated for future Muslim generations until Judgement Day, represents a mainstream view; this is Spencer's account, not a survey. Al-Hussaini says no religious-law ground exists to think God's promise was broken. Both essays were commissioned by the Middle East Quarterly, whose publisher takes a position on the conflict.

could_not_verify: Whether some Muslims dispute identifying the 'farthest mosque' of 17:1 with Jerusalem: no Muslim source making that argument was found; only the Middle East Quarterly editors' statement that it is 'generally interpreted' as Jerusalem is quoted.
A survey or poll of how many Muslim scholars read the promise as lapsed or as lasting: none found; the card names the scholars it quotes and does not say what share hold either view.

Muhammad Asad and Wahbah al-Zuhayli on 5:21: no readable page found, so not cited. Sayyid Qutb's commentary (read) says the land was 'forbidden to that particular generation' on 'the weightier view'; that is not quoted because it does not address whether the promise lapsed.
The Quran's counter-verses that Saqr cites (21:105, 7:167) and that Jewish readers may expect (7:168) are not quoted from the verse pages.
Spencer's claim that most Muslims reject a Jewish claim, and the Hamas charter's reading, are in a contested entry because no survey or second source for 'most Muslims' was found.

Palazzi's own Tablet essay (403 to the reader) was not read; only First Things' summary of it, which is a blog note, and al-Adwan's interview is read only through The Algemeiner's relay of a Mida magazine interview.
Muslim commentaries beyond the three used per verse (Ibn Kathir, al-Jalalayn, Tanwir al-Miqbas): al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi on 7:137, 10:93 and 17:104 were not found in readable English.

Which Muslim voice on the lapsed reading addresses 5:21 directly beyond Saqr and Saad: the Jordanian Iftaa' article does not discuss 5:21 and is cited only for the Israelites losing 'the honor of the trust'.
First-hand texts for al-Adwan (the Mida interview) and Palazzi (his Tablet essay): the card holds a news relay and a blurb.

Scripture facts (Quran 5:21, 5:22-24, 5:26, 7:137, 10:93, 17:104; Genesis 17:8 and 17:21) are worded as what the text says, with the text itself as the record. The 'readers' are other editions or translations of the same text (Quranx, the Quranic Arabic Corpus, BibleGateway, eBible), which confirm that we copied it correctly; they are not independent opinions. Which reading of the text is right is not a fact on this card and belongs to contested.

The answer does not rest on al-Adwan or Palazzi: both are read only second-hand (The Algemeiner's relay of a Mida magazine interview; First Things' summary of a Tablet essay whose page could not be read, including through the Wayback Machine). Fact 11 keeps them, marked as reported. A person should read Palazzi's essay 'Allah Is a Zionist' (Tablet, 18 March 2010) and the Mida interview with al-Adwan.
Facts that do not meet the gate's source rule: none by count. Fact 11 (the 'lasting' reading) has one first-hand voice (al-Hussaini); the other two are second-hand and the gate counts their relays.

FINAL REVIEW (2026-11-20): record rule. Facts 0 to 5 and 13 are worded only as what the verse says and the record was read (quran.com verse pages, Mechon Mamre) with the verse before and after. But the 'readers' (Quranx, the Quranic Arabic Corpus, BibleGateway, eBible) are other editions or translations of the same text, not readers; the only real readers of what 5:21 says are the commentaries on facts 6 to 9. The gate counts the editions; I do not. A person should decide whether independent translations by named translators are enough for a scripture record fact, or add a scholarly reader. Fact 12 (Jerusalem and al-Aqsa): Quran 17:1 does not name Jerusalem and the hadith names al-Aqsa only; the identification and the qibla rest on ReligionFacts (no named author, relabelled 'other'), so the fact now has two reliable sources. Fact 4: the card cited 5:24 only but said 5:22-24; reworded to 5:24.
not_claimed: That scripture settles a modern political question: who should govern the land, or what borders, is not answered by the verses quoted.
That any reading of these verses is the correct Islamic one; the card reports what the text says and what Muslim scholars have said.
That the Israelites' tie to the land rests on the Quran: Jewish ties rest on Jewish sources and history (see the Jewish presence card).
That Muslim attachment to Jerusalem is weaker or newer because the Quran does not name the city.

skeptic.notes: Final review after the record rule. Read quran.com 5:21, 5:22, 5:24, 5:26, 7:137, 10:93, 17:104 and 17:1 in context: the texts match the facts. Saqr on About Islam (the quoted 'promise stands so long as ...' and 'they will never remain there forever' are on the page, and the fatwa hopes for 'another defeat and severe blow'; the card says so), the Jordanian Iftaa' article (Noah Ali Salman: 'final outcome belongs to the righteous', framed as 'the end of the battle between us and the Jews'), Saad (About Islam) and al-Hussaini (MEQ). Record flags: wording is honest on every flagged fact (each says what the verse says, not what it means). But the record rule is not met in substance: the two 'readers' are other editions of the same text (the writer admits it), so no scripture fact has a reader (must-fix, or a person decides translations by different named translators suffice). Fixed by me: (should-fix, done) fact 4 said 5:22-24 but cites 5:24; now 5:24. (should-fix, done) fact 13 said 'not Ishmael', which is a reading (Genesis 17:20 blesses Ishmael); now only what 17:8 and 17:21 say. (should-fix, done) ReligionFacts relabelled 'other' (no named author or institution). Still open: (must-fix) fact 11 (the 'lasting' reading) has one first-hand voice (al-Hussaini); al-Adwan and Palazzi are second-hand (relays), as the card says; (should-fix) fact 10: Saqr and Saad are on one site and the Jordanian article does not discuss 5:21; (should-fix) fact 12 identification of the farthest mosque with Jerusalem has no scholarly or Muslim source on the card; (nit) fact 3's 17:104 has three translators giving different renderings, now stated. Heard (al-Habbash) is a fair version. Strongest objection from Muslims: the 'lasting' voices are second-hand and one runs through a pro-Israel outlet, and no survey says which reading is commoner. From Jewish readers: Saqr's fatwa, the card's main 'lapsed' voice, also predicts the Jews' defeat. Status stays draft.
